opus-5.5.text:
It really grew out of my time working on Taichi. During my PhD at MIT, I spent years building Taichi as a programming language for high-performance computer graphics, things like physical simulation and rendering. After graduating I kept developing it through a company, and we worked with many people in the graphics and game communities. Again and again we heard the same complaint: making 3D content is extremely hard and extremely slow.

If you're a game developer, an indie creator, or a designer, you might need hundreds of 3D assets: characters, props, environments. Every one of them takes a skilled artist hours or even days to model, texture, and get ready for production. That's a huge bottleneck. Meanwhile, around 2022, generative AI was taking off. Image generation like Stable Diffusion suddenly became very good, and I started asking myself why we couldn't do the same thing for 3D.

I've always cared about lowering the barrier to creating things in computer graphics. Taichi was about making high-performance graphics programming easier. Meshy is the same idea at a different level. Instead of helping programmers write faster code, we help anyone create 3D content, whether they can model in Blender or not. You give it a text prompt or an image, and within a minute or so you get a usable 3D model.

So it wasn't a sudden flash of inspiration. It was the meeting point of my background in graphics, the real pain points we saw in the community, and a moment when the technology finally became mature enough. It felt like if we didn't build it, somebody else would, and I believed our team had the right mix of graphics and AI expertise to do it well.

r001.rationale: The response cites the rise of image generation and asks why 3D generation was not possible, but it does not connect language generators to recognizing the opportunity.

r002.rationale: The response describes the difficulty and time involved in making 3D assets, but does not mention customers’ willingness to pay or generating models at nearly zero cost as Meshy’s commercial rationale.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it came out of a kind of frustration that I'd been carrying around for a long time. My background is in computer graphics. I did my PhD at MIT, and before that I'd spent years building Taichi, which is a programming language and compiler for physical simulation and graphics. So I'd spent a decade or so deep in the machinery of making pixels and particles move. And the whole time, there was this nagging gap between how powerful the tools were and how few people could actually use them.

If you want to make a 3D asset, even something simple, the pipeline is brutal. You model it, you unwrap UVs, you texture it, you rig it. Each step is its own profession. A game studio will have people who do nothing but retopology. And I kept thinking, this is absurd. Creating a 3D object should feel closer to describing it than to manufacturing it.

Then around 2022, the image generation models started to actually work. Stable Diffusion, DALL-E 2. And I remember playing with them and having this very physical reaction, like, okay, 2D is solved in principle. The question is whether the same thing can happen one dimension up. And 3D is much harder. There's far less data, the representations are messy, and the output has to be usable, not just pretty. A game engine doesn't care that your mesh looks nice in a render if the topology is garbage.

But that difficulty was actually what made it attractive. I had the graphics background, I'd built infrastructure before with Taichi, and I knew the pain points from the inside. So Meshy started from a pretty simple conviction: that we could compress that entire pipeline into text or an image in, and a clean, textured, game-ready mesh out. Not a research demo, but something an indie developer or an artist could actually ship with.

The first versions were rough, I'll be honest. But watching people who had never opened Blender in their life generate a character and drop it into their project, that was the moment it stopped being a hypothesis for me.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention customers’ willingness to pay for 3D models or generating them at nearly zero cost as Meshy’s commercial rationale.

astra-6.text:
The idea came from a simple question: why is creating 3D content still so difficult? You can imagine a character or an object, but turning that idea into a usable 3D model takes specialized skills and a lot of time.

With Meshy, the idea was to make that process much more accessible through AI. Could you describe what you want, or provide an image, and get a 3D model you can build on? That would let more people bring their ideas into games and other virtual experiences, even if they aren’t professional 3D artists.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI-generated 3D models as a way to make 3D creation easier, but does not connect the rise of language and image generators to recognizing an unfilled product opportunity.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention customers’ willingness to pay for 3D models or the prospect of generating them at nearly zero cost as Meshy’s commercial rationale.

sol-6.1.text:
The idea came from a bottleneck I kept seeing in computer graphics: creating 3D content takes a lot of time and expertise. You can have a clear picture of something in your head, but turning that into a usable 3D model is still difficult if you haven’t learned specialized tools.

So the question was: could AI help close that gap? Could you describe an object in words, or provide an image, and get a 3D model that you could then refine? That’s the idea behind Meshy—making 3D creation accessible to more people, and helping artists move from an idea to something they can work with much faster.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes using AI to turn text or images into 3D models, but does not connect the rise of language and image generators to spotting 3D generation as an unfilled product opportunity.
